blocks.content: Everything the file allocation and disk scheduling chapters describe ultimately runs on top of a real, physical storage medium, and today that medium is almost always one of two fundamentally different technologies: the traditional spinning hard disk, HDD, or the newer, electrically based solid state drive, SSD. This chapter looks underneath the file system entirely, at the hardware itself, and explains exactly why these two behave so differently.

Understanding this hardware layer retroactively explains a lot of earlier material: why seek time was worth an entire chapter of scheduling algorithms, and why those same algorithms mean almost nothing on modern SSD based laptops and phones.
1. How a Hard Disk Drive Physically Works
blocks.text: 1. How a Hard Disk Drive Physically Works

blocks.content: An HDD stores data on one or more spinning magnetic platters. A mechanical arm, with a read write head mounted on its end, physically moves across the surface of a platter to reach the track holding the requested data, then waits for the platter own rotation to bring the correct sector underneath the head before any actual reading or writing happens.

This design, entirely mechanical at its core, directly explains the seek time concept from the disk scheduling chapter: since a physical arm genuinely has to travel, and travel takes real time, the order in which pending requests are serviced has a real, measurable effect on total performance. Nothing about an HDD access is instantaneous, every single operation waits on real, physical movement first.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197367-469977062.png
blocks.alt: How a Hard Disk Drive Physically Works

blocks.content: 2. How a Solid State Drive Physically Works
blocks.text: 2. How a Solid State Drive Physically Works

blocks.content: An SSD has no moving parts whatsoever. Data is stored electrically, in flash memory cells organized into pages, which are grouped into larger blocks. A controller chip addresses any cell it needs directly and electrically, with no arm to move and no platter that needs to finish rotating first.

This is precisely why SSD access times are roughly uniform, regardless of where on the drive the requested data physically sits. There is no concept of one location being physically closer to a current head position than another, because there is no head and no position in the mechanical sense at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197368-274231089.png
blocks.alt: How a Solid State Drive Physically Works

4. Why Seek Time Is a Meaningless Concept on SSDs
blocks.text: 4. Why Seek Time Is a Meaningless Concept on SSDs

blocks.content: The entire disk scheduling chapter, FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, was built around one single goal: minimizing the physical travel distance of a mechanical read write head across a spinning platter. An SSD simply has no such head, and therefore nothing analogous to travel distance to minimize at all.

This means those classic scheduling algorithms provide little to no real benefit when applied to an SSD. SSD controllers instead face an entirely different set of internal concerns, covered next, that have no real HDD equivalent, centered specifically around how flash memory can and cannot be written to.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197368-41547204.png
blocks.alt: Why Seek Time Is a Meaningless Concept on SSDs

blocks.content: 5. The SSD Write Limitation: Erase Before Write
blocks.text: 5. The SSD Write Limitation: Erase Before Write

blocks.content: This is the single most important SSD specific concept in this chapter. Unlike an HDD, where a magnetic sector can simply be overwritten in place with new data, a flash memory cell cannot be directly overwritten once it holds data. The entire block containing that cell must first be erased before any new data can be written into it.

Compounding this, each individual flash cell can only endure a limited number of total erase cycles before it physically wears out and becomes unreliable. This is a fundamentally different kind of constraint than anything an HDD faces, an HDD magnetic surface does not meaningfully degrade from being overwritten repeatedly the way a flash cell does from being erased repeatedly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197368-858630251.png
blocks.alt: The SSD Write Limitation: Erase Before Write

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785409197368-709941553.png
blocks.alt: The SSD Write Limitation: Erase Before Write

blocks.title: Why this matters so much
blocks.content: If an SSD naively rewrote the exact same physical cells over and over, for a frequently updated file for instance, those specific cells would wear out and fail far earlier than the rest of the drive, even while the drive as a whole still had plenty of healthy capacity left.
6. Wear Leveling: The Real World Fix
blocks.text: 6. Wear Leveling: The Real World Fix

blocks.content: Wear leveling is the SSD controller own solution to the erase cycle limitation. Rather than repeatedly writing to the same physical cells whenever a particular piece of logical data gets updated, the controller deliberately spreads writes evenly across all the physical cells on the drive over time.

The controller maintains an internal mapping between the logical addresses the file system thinks it is writing to and the actual, constantly shifting physical cells that data really lives in. This is precisely what allows the drive to avoid any one region wearing out and failing far earlier than the rest, meaningfully extending the overall usable lifetime of the drive.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197369-960138393.png
blocks.alt: Wear Leveling: The Real World Fix

blocks.content: 7. TRIM: An OS Level SSD Optimization
blocks.text: 7. TRIM: An OS Level SSD Optimization

blocks.content: TRIM is a command the operating system sends to an SSD specifically, with no real HDD equivalent or need, informing the drive controller which blocks are no longer actually in use by the file system, typically right after a file is deleted.

Without this information, an SSD controller has no way to know a given block content is genuinely garbage rather than still meaningful data, and cannot safely erase it ahead of time. With TRIM, the controller can proactively erase those now unused blocks in the background, well before anything actually needs to be written there, making the eventual write to that space noticeably faster when it happens.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197369-927888474.png
blocks.alt: TRIM: An OS Level SSD Optimization

8. The Same Operation, Two Different Machines
blocks.text: 8. The Same Operation, Two Different Machines

blocks.content: Overwriting an existing file data makes the contrast concrete. On an HDD, the head simply seeks to the sectors that already hold the old data and writes the new magnetic data directly in place, the same physical location as before, just with different content now recorded on it.

On an SSD, the controller typically cannot overwrite the existing flash cells directly at all. Instead it writes the new data to a different location that has already been erased and ready to receive it, and updates its internal mapping table so future reads for that logical data find it at its new physical location, the exact mechanism wear leveling depends on to keep spreading writes around the drive.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409197369-889508603.png
blocks.alt: The Same Operation, Two Different Machines

blocks.content: 9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming an SSD is simply a faster HDD with no other real architectural differences, when the erase before write limitation and wear leveling are fundamentally different concerns with no real HDD analog at all.","Assuming disk scheduling algorithms like SCAN or C-SCAN still meaningfully improve performance on SSDs, when the seek time they were built to minimize essentially does not exist there.","Forgetting that overwriting data on an SSD typically means writing to a new location and remapping, not updating the original cells in place the way an HDD does."]
items: Assuming an SSD is simply a faster HDD with no other real architectural differences, when the erase before write limitation and wear leveling are fundamentally different concerns with no real HDD analog at all.
Assuming disk scheduling algorithms like SCAN or C-SCAN still meaningfully improve performance on SSDs, when the seek time they were built to minimize essentially does not exist there.
Forgetting that overwriting data on an SSD typically means writing to a new location and remapping, not updating the original cells in place the way an HDD does.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain the erase before write limitation and wear leveling from memory, this is one of the most commonly asked storage systems interview topics, and a genuinely strong answer connects it back to why the SSD controller has to maintain its own internal address mapping in the first place.

This closes out the hardware layer for the File Systems and Storage module. From the file abstraction itself, through directories, inodes, allocation methods, journaling for crash consistency, disk scheduling, and now the physical medium underneath all of it, the next and final chapter looks at RAID, combining multiple physical drives together for better reliability and performance.
